messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Please help speeding up STAN code
parts:
You need to constrain all your parameters to match those
uniform distributions. Then you can drop the uniform.

> parameters {
> real<lower=0, upper=1> aa;
> real<lower=0> bb;
> real<lower=0, upper=1> cc;
> real<lower=0, upper=1> dd;
> real<lower=0, upper=1> ee;
> real ff;
> real<lower=0> gg;
> real ss;
> }

> model{
> aa ~ uniform(0,1) ;
> bb ~ normal(500, 150);
> cc ~ uniform(0,1) ;
> dd ~ uniform(0,1) ;
> ee ~ uniform(0,1) ;
> ff ~ uniform(-2,2) ;
> gg ~ uniform(0,3) ;
> ss ~ uniform(-5,5) ;
>
> stream ~ lognormal(log(Rt), exp(ss)) ;
> }"

This

> stream ~ lognormal(log(Rt), exp(ss)) ;

is probably wrong, because of the way the density for the lognormal
is defined, which takes the log of the mu value (so here you get
log of Rt done twice.

Also, you can define ss as a positive constrained variable rather
than needing to exponentiate it.

You have conditionals based on parameters. You need to make
sure that the results are continuously differentiable, which they
almost never are with this kind of structure. How did you code
them in JAGS given that it doesn't allow conditional statements?

It's odd to have normal(500, 150) for a variable with lower bound
of zero, as it's going to truncate some non-trivial amount of the
mass and won't correspond to a proper generative model. Also,
it'w oudl be better to take

bb_raw ~ normal(0, 1);

bb <- 500 + 150 * bb_raw;

to keep all the parameters on the unit scale to the extent possible.

Unless motivated by physical constraints, we don't recommend these
uniform bounded priors as they can be bad for both the computation
and the statistical properties --- they don't do what most people think
they are going to do in practice (namely truncating probability mass
and skewing the posterior means).

If any of those variables defined in transformed parameters only
involve variables declared as data, then they should be moved to
the transformed data block.

Also, you don't want to measure time per iteration but
effective sample size per second, because you only need
to run (either JAGS or Stan) until you get a large enough
effective sample size for all parameters.

- Bob

Thank you Bob Carpenter

I appreciate it. I should search proper priors instead of uniform priors.

Best,



2016년 8월 10일 수요일 오후 1시 7분 6초 UTC-4, Kuk-Hyun Ahn 님의 말:

Dear Stan Mailing List,

I am relatively new for stan. I am changing my JAGS's code to stan. 

While changing a code, I exprienced very slow speed for running the code in stan.

Could you give some advice to increase the speed? 

When I used JAGS, it tooks 30 minimutes for 5000 iterations including 3000 burn-ins with 2 chains.

But it took six hours with stan.

Probably there are some ineffective codes.


I really do appreciate the help from this exceptional group.

Many thanks,

###################################################

model <- "
data {
  int<lower=0> N;
  real stream[N];
  real preci[N];
  real temp[N];
  real poevp[N];
}

parameters {
 real<lower=0, upper=1> aa;
 real<lower=0>          bb;
 real<lower=0, upper=1> cc;
 real<lower=0, upper=1> dd;
 real<lower=0, upper=1> ee;
 real                   ff;
 real<lower=0>          gg;
 real                   ss;
}

transformed parameters {
  vector[N] At;
  vector[N] Mt;
  vector[N] Pef;
  vector[N] ETef;
  vector[N] SNOW;
  vector[N] St;
  vector[N] Gt;
  vector[N] Rt;
  vector[N] Yt;
  vector[N] Wt;
  vector[N] Et;

  At[1] <- 0;
  Mt[1] <- 0;
  Pef[1]  <- preci[1];
  ETef[1] <- poevp[1];
  SNOW[1] <- 0;
  St[1] <- 200;
  Gt[1] <- 200;
  Rt[1] <- stream[1];
  Yt[1] <- 0;
  Wt[1] <- 0;
  Et[1] <- 0;

for (i in 2:N) {                           ;
  SNOW[i] <- (ff - temp[i])/(gg)           ;

  if (temp[i] >= (ff-gg) && temp[i] <= ff) {
  Mt[i] <- ((At[i-1] + preci[i]*SNOW[i])*ee*(1-SNOW[i])) ;
  Pef[i] <- (preci[i]*(1 - SNOW[i]) + Mt[i])             ;
  ETef[i] <- 0                                           ;
  At[i] <- ((At[i-1] + preci[i]*SNOW[i]) - Mt[i])        ;

  } else if (temp[i] > ff) {
  Mt[i] <- ((At[i-1]))        ;
  Pef[i] <- (preci[i]+Mt[i])  ;
  ETef[i] <- poevp[i]         ;
  At[i] <- At[i-1] - Mt[i]    ;

  } else {
  Mt[i] <- 0                  ;
  Pef[i] <- 0                 ;
  ETef[i] <- 0                ;
  At[i] <- At[i-1]+preci[i]   ;
  }

  Wt[i] <- Pef[i] + St[i-1]                    ;
  Yt[i] <- (Wt[i]+bb)/(2*aa) - sqrt(((Wt[i]+bb)/(2*aa))^2-(Wt[i]*bb/aa)) ;
  St[i] <- Yt[i]*exp(-1*ETef[i]/bb)            ;
  Et[i] <- Yt[i]*(1-exp(-1*(ETef[i]/bb)))      ;
  Gt[i] <- (Gt[i-1] + cc*(Wt[i]-Yt[i]))/(1+dd) ;
  Rt[i] <- ((1-cc)*(Wt[i]-Yt[i])+dd*Gt[i])     ;
}                                              ;
}

model{
  aa ~ uniform(0,1)   ;
  bb ~ normal(500, 150);
  cc ~ uniform(0,1)   ;
  dd ~ uniform(0,1)   ;
  ee ~ uniform(0,1)   ;
  ff ~ uniform(-2,2)  ;
  gg ~ uniform(0,3)   ;
  ss ~ uniform(-5,5) ;

  stream ~ lognormal(log(Rt), exp(ss)) ;
}"

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Please help speeding up STAN code
parts:
The uniform priors on constrained intervals are proper in
the sense that they integrate to 1. They're just not what
we recommend for anything other than "physically" constrained
parameters, such as the parameter to a binomial.

We have a wiki and lots of advice in the manual chapter on
regression:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Prior-Choice-Recommendations

- Bob
